question: A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. analysis: The clinical presentation of the patient, including bilateral papilledema, headache, and transient visual disturbances, is suggestive of increased intracranial pressure. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), also known as pseudotumor cerebri, is a condition that can present with these symptoms. A lumbar puncture is the definitive test to confirm the diagnosis of IIH, as it can measure the opening pressure of the cerebrospinal fluid, which is typically elevated in this condition. Other tests, such as MRI, are useful to rule out other causes of increased intracranial pressure but do not confirm IIH.
